slides.title: Existing Standards and Solution Approaches for Multicast Routing
Benefits and Challenges of MOQ over Multicast QUIC

chat.author: Kyle Rose
chat.text: This is far too into the weeds technically. We need specifically to avoid solutioning here.

chat.author: Lars Eggert
chat.text: I arrived late and I should probably know this, but I don't: is this BOF WG-forming?

chat.author: Lucas Pardue
chat.text: This is a non-WG forming BoF

chat.author: Kyle Rose
chat.text: The goal here is to decide whether there is interest in working on this problem space, and to take the feedback to decide on what the next step should be, whether that's dispatch to an existing WG, setting up a WG-forming BoF, or something else.

chat.author: Kyle Rose
chat.text: :drum:

chat.author: Christian Huitema
chat.text: I think there is an integration issue. A multicast stream is defined by an IP address to which the client subscribe, and a port number. That pretty much means as many UDP sockets as multicast chennels, which is significantly different from "just one socket" in basic QUIC.

chat.author: Giovanni Marzot
chat.text: yes, yes, yes, yes

chat.author: Christian Huitema
chat.text: yes

chat.author: Daniel Bernier
chat.text: Question I have is : have we listed potential problems of default MOQ and use of relays that would justify running MOQ over MCAST ?

chat.author: Titouan Soulard
chat.text: What is the mailing list Greg Shepherd was referring to where the "Flexicast QUIC" application was posted? I searched for SQUAD ML, but does not seem to exist.

chat.author: Louis Navarre
chat.text: Either the QUIC or MBONE mailing list

chat.author: Lucas Pardue
chat.text: @Daniel I think Magnus' presentation will speak to MOQ plus multicast

chat.author: Titouan Soulard
chat.text: Right, mboned, found it, thanks!

chat.author: Jonathan Lennox
chat.text: I'm trying to figure out - do people think that HTTP/3 with multicast (for HLS/DASH presumably) would be practical, or is this only sensible for MOQ?

chat.author: Sean Turner
chat.text: Flexicast actually went to both ;)

chat.author: Martin Duke
chat.text: I'm glad to hear that there are some worked solutions being evaluated

chat.author: Titouan Soulard
chat.text: Oh, now I read Louis' message differently indeed

chat.author: Watson Ladd
chat.text: I'd be interested in understand what has to change: e.g. if we throw in FEC or fountain codes does that then impact client assumptions about things like resuming downloads while helping with bandwidth usage and avoiding unicast fallback

chat.author: Lucas Pardue
chat.text: that would be a good question to bring to the mic in the discussion section Watson

chat.author: Christian Huitema
chat.text: FEC is great in these scenarios if losses at clients are independent. But yes, you want the transport to know the fraction of packets that would have been lost without FEC.

chat.author: Watson Ladd
chat.text: if you drop a whole chunk up the tree, everyone can reconstruct (I assume doing the usual RS erasure stuff) avoiding a unicast recovery hoard

chat.author: Louis Navarre
chat.text: Thanks for the DRIAD idea, we will look into this!

chat.author: Kyle Rose
chat.text:
Martin Duke said:

I'm glad to hear that there are some worked solutions being evaluated

Yeah, sorry, I was being a bit wishy-washy about that. I was trying overly hard to be careful not to give the impression that we're shopping around a final, fully-packaged solution to get a stamp of approval. But we do have something we believe works, at least for many of the situations we've identified, and we have clear ideas on how we could deal with the others even if those have not been developed into experimental code yet.

chat.author: Martin Thomson
chat.text: magnus' point about packet numbers is not one that I had considered.  Consider also how you signal how a multicast delivery correlates with unicast flows more generally.  How does the current set of proposals manage this?

chat.author: Christian Huitema
chat.text: @watson: my point is that all receivers loose the same packet, then adding redondancy once over multicast is obviously better than sending N copies. But if different receivers loose different packets, then N+P redundancy over multicast is also a big win.

chat.author: Christian Huitema
chat.text: @martin: if you do mutipath, tere is a sequence number per pat.

chat.author: Daniel Bernier
chat.text: so one angle where Multicast might become advantageous is "if" we end up with a MOQ Relay platforms that become  just a new flavor of Media CDNs (bloated, no real interop).

chat.author: Louis Navarre
chat.text: @Martin, with Flexicast using Multipath underneath, the multicast "path" uses a different packet number space, so completely different from the per-receiver unicast used packet numbers. The correlation happens at the stream-level, if any

chat.author: Daniel Bernier
chat.text: if we keep relays light then the challenge will be different

chat.author: Martin Thomson
chat.text: QUIC does not guarantee that the same data is not sent twice.

chat.author: Martin Thomson
chat.text: Well, at most once is a QUIC datagram property.  QUIC streams do at least once.

chat.author: Martin Thomson
Louis Navarre
chat.text: @Martin, I am sorry I am not sure to get the question. For me this is a multipath-related question because the relationship between the multicast path and the unicast path is the same as in multipath, isn't it? (And, in the case of Flexicast, the receiver sends PATH_ACK to the source similarly to multipath). But I may miss something here

chat.author: Jonathan Lennox
chat.text: Yeah, the multicast file distribution case is going to need new application-layer protocols - I don't see how you could make HTTP/3  as it is today fit with it unless you can guarantee that all the receivers start the download simultaneously.

chat.author: Jonathan Lennox
chat.text: That said, an HTTP extension that delivers large files out-of-order in chunks doesn't seem that complex or to do that much damage to HTTP semantics.

chat.author: Craig Taylor
chat.text:
I see none of the walled garden operators in the room or at the mic; Anyone in the chat?
It would be great for them to voice the current operational challenges, and perceptions of opening up...

chat.author: Louis Navarre
chat.text: @Jonathan, in our research we looked at this problem by splitting the file into blocks, and send them in a carousel manner like FLUTE does. Again, not saying that it's the best solution, but it worked in our research :) if you are interested, we wrote a scientific paper about it

chat.author: Christian Huitema
chat.text: The pointy hammer analogy comes to mind. The propoal here is to build a new tool, an extension to the transport layer that may or may not be used by many applications. A pointy hammer, when applications could just use bespoke tools that actually meet their needs.

chat.author: Martin Thomson
chat.text: Thinking of solutions at different layers: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-reschke-http-oob-encoding/09/

chat.author: Martin Thomson
François Michel
chat.text: I don’t think we should limit ourselves to multicast IP. Multicast quic can work over unicast IP, we can just duplicate quic packets to several multicast endpoints. You still avoid encoding and encrypting the packet n times.

chat.author: Alan Frindell
chat.text: That's helpful, though actually sending the packets is also costly.

chat.author: Watson Ladd
chat.text: Is the WiFi issue just MIMO can't beamform because too few antennas vs beams when doing simultaneous things?

chat.author: Louis Navarre
chat.text: @Martin, Ok I get the point. It's true that so far we have found ad hoc solutions, like playing with the stream identifiers, but we need something more generic. Thanks for pointing it out.

chat.author: Martin Thomson
François Michel
chat.text: @Watson: that’s one thing. Another issue is that the access point needs to support  several receiver with different capabilities. It therefore limits the sending rate to 6Mbps in general, which is extremely low.

chat.author: Martin Thomson
chat.text: Magnus' point about the MoQ object hierarchy and repair there highlighted that you can't necessarily bank on a stable identity that is visible to the transport/QUIC layer.

chat.author: Louis Navarre
chat.text: Thanks for the comment. We will clarify that for the next version of the draft.

chat.author: Martin Thomson
chat.text:
I also want to share a quote, the first sentence of RFC 8999:

QUIC is a connection-oriented protocol between two endpoints.

Ask then whether you think that this is QUIC or some other protocol.

chat.author: François Michel
chat.text: Which is the mailing list gorry is talking about?

chat.author: Craig Taylor
chat.text: Did you catch that François - quic mailing list

chat.author: François Michel
chat.text: Yup. Thanks!

chat.author: Christian Huitema
chat.text: If we do anything, it should be as small as possible, so applications can customise how they use it.

chat.author: Craig Taylor
chat.text: I'm still concerned we heard from none of the walled garden operators.

chat.author: Louis Navarre
chat.text: Thank you for all the comments!
